input.question: If our atmosphere was 78% Oxygen instead of nitrogen, would we be able to hold our breath longer?
input.ground_truth: If we hadn't been killed off by fires raging across continents every time there was a lightning storm, or exterminated by gigantic insects, sure. P.S. Insects are limited in size by their relatively inefficient pulmonary systems (and, possibly, their exoskeletons).

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: If our atmosphere was 78% Oxygen instead of nitrogen, would we be able to hold our breath longer?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big jar of air. Right now, most of the air in that jar is called “nitrogen,” and only a little bit is “oxygen,” which is what helps you breathe and stay alive.

But let’s pretend that instead of mostly nitrogen, the jar is mostly oxygen.

Now, when you hold your breath, your body is using up the oxygen in your blood, and it makes you want to breathe again when it runs low.

If the air around you is mostly oxygen, that doesn’t mean you have more oxygen inside your body when you hold your breath. The oxygen inside your body is what matters, and it gets used up at the same speed, no matter what’s in the air around you.

So, having more oxygen in the air outside doesn’t help you hold your breath longer. Your body still runs out of oxygen inside, so you still have to breathe soon!

So, the answer is: No, we wouldn’t be able to hold our breath longer if the air was mostly oxygen.
